newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss firms play down importance of cloned sheep.
newsitem.headline: Swiss firms play down importance of cloned sheep.

text.p: Swiss pharmaceutical executives underscored on Wednesday their commitment to refrain from genetic experiments on humans and played down the importance of British scientists' cloning of an adult sheep.

"We have no such experiments at Swiss companies," Thomas Cueni, general secretary of Interpharma, the association of Swiss companies performing pharmaceutical research, said of scientists' ability to duplicate perfectly a sheep.

"We have determined after discussing this with researchers at our companies that the firms' expectations are very subdued about the significance of what has happened," he added at a news conference on health care reform in Switzerland.

Cueni said the experiment was interesting from a scientific point of view, but added animal-protection law that balances the potential benefit of such research against possible risks and ethical factors would determine how to proceed in Switzerland.
Cueni stressed that the cloning of the sheep had to be clearly differentiated from cloning people, which is expressly banned in Switzerland and elsewhere in Europe.
Interpharma vice president Franz Humer, who is also chief operating officer at Roche Holding AG, underscored this point.

"It is important to note that we categorically speak out very clearly against research on embryos and against cloning of people. We also speak out against intervening in human genetic material," he said.
"This is also anchored as a ban in the federal constitution, and we stand squarely behind this ban."

Humer warned Swiss voters they would cripple Swiss research if they adopt by referendum a proposed "genetic protection initiatve" that would ban almost all forms of genetic experiments and genetically altered products.
